assessmentSummary.identity: One bilateral standing forearm wall-slide cycle with a required terminal full-arm lift-off. Begin facing a smooth wall with both vertical forearms shoulder-width apart on the wall, elbows near 90 degrees, feet fixed, and trunk organized. Maintain bilateral forearm contact while sliding upward into the declared comfortable overhead range, extend the elbows as range permits, lift both arms and forearms clear of the wall without moving the feet or borrowing lumbar extension, replace both forearms on the wall, and slide to the same start. One complete return is one repetition. Comfortable range, foot distance or stance, lift-off amplitude, tempo, brief pauses, breathing prompts, repetitions, sets, rest, and a stable forearm comfort layer are annotations. Omitting lift-off, changing the sliding interface, adding resistance, changing base or laterality, using a roller, adding another action, or performing assessment changes the task.
currentCardFindings: Source 35 and consolidated Source 899 retain two selectable skeletal variants and two incomplete profiles even though the names and exact forearm-slide-plus-lift-off mechanics are one identity.
The source description makes lift-off optional and says hands or forearms, so it does not define a reproducible terminal contact rule or one-repetition cycle.

Source 1309 was consolidated by name through archived Source 899 even though its throwing-context card omits exact wall contacts, slide path, lift-off mechanics, and count. That chain is not evidence of exact identity and must remain nonselectable and quarantined.

The legacy age floor of eight, publication state, generic dose, sparse 20/10/20 score, and five unreviewed media rows lack card-specific calibration, playback, exactness, accessibility, quality, safety, and approval evidence.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when a smooth wall, safe standing station, bilateral forearm slide, required terminal full-arm lift-off, shoulder and elbow range, trunk control, symptoms, dose, duration, and cumulative overhead, shoulder, scapular, and trunk-control budgets fit. Do not silently omit the lift-off or change the wall interface, resistance, base, laterality, equipment, action sequence, clinical scope, or count. Recompute logistics, duration, fatigue, substitutions, persistence, and coach and athlete rendering after any change.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Direct Physitrack and Catalyst lift-off instructions, peer-reviewed wall-slide EMG and resistance-position studies, a small condition-specific wall-slide trial used only as an outcome boundary, a rotator-cuff-tendinopathy clinical-practice scope boundary, current YouTube oEmbed metadata, and comparison with exact no-lift-off reach, foam-roller, wall-angel, wall-push-up-plus, prone-Y, resisted, and incompletely specified throwing neighbors
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: No source validates one universal wall distance, shoulder angle, forearm pressure, lift-off height, scapular position, muscle force, activation target, dose, frequency, recovery interval, prevention or treatment result, progression order, or Vortex score. General wall-slide studies do not validate the terminal lift-off phase, and no media candidate has been watched in full.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Stand facing a wall with forearms on the wall. Gently press into the wall, slide the forearms upward, then at the top lift the hands or forearms slightly away while keeping ribs down. Return with control.

claims: Physitrack specifies standing facing a wall, vertical shoulder-width forearms on the wall, an upward forearm slide, a top arm lift-off, replacement of the forearms, and return to start.
Vortex fixes the bilateral contact, terminal full-arm clearance, fixed-foot, trunk-control, and return-to-start count boundaries without claiming one universal range.
Catalyst describes parallel forearms against a smooth wall, upward sliding, full extension, straight-arm lift-off, and controlled return.
Brace, push, and reach are controlled planning terms rather than source-authored outcome guarantees.

evidence.sourceTitle: A comparison of serratus anterior muscle activation during a wall slide exercise and other traditional exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
claims: A wall-slide study measured serratus anterior activity at 90, 120, and 140 degrees of humeral elevation and found activity increased with elevation.
The study supports shoulder-elevation and scapular-muscle involvement but did not test this exact terminal lift-off or establish isolated activation, force, normal range, or eligibility.

evidence.sourceTitle: Theraband Applications for Improved Upper Extremity Wall-Slide Exercises
claims: The laboratory protocol standardized scapular-plane shoulder flexion, elbow flexion, ulnar-forearm wall contact, ascent, hold, and descent.
It tested regular and banded wall slides without the exact lift-off, so it supports contact, plane, phase, and resistance boundaries rather than the complete Source 35 identity.
The direct task adds a controlled straight-arm lift-off after the supported slide while the trunk remains braced.
The 30/16/30 proposal describes this exercise task only and requires independent calibration; it is not a participant skill or age level.

evidence.sourceTitle: A comparison of serratus anterior muscle activation during a wall slide exercise and other traditional exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Wall slides produce angle-dependent serratus anterior activity under low external loading.
Track complete cycles, terminal lift-off seconds, wall-contact seconds, faults, symptoms, and overlapping overhead work; tissue thresholds and recovery hours remain planning estimates.

evidence.sourceTitle: Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy Diagnosis, Nonsurgical Medical Care, and Rehabilitation: A Clinical Practice Guideline
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
claims: The clinical guideline addresses assessment, treatment, prognosis, and return to function for adults with suspected rotator-cuff tendinopathy.
A workout card cannot diagnose, treat, clear return to sport, or replace individualized clinical care; symptom, post-trauma, neurologic, and scope escalation remains mandatory.
Catalyst gives a preparatory example of one to three sets of eight to ten repetitions.
That example is not a universal prescription and does not validate Vortex duration, budget, frequency, recovery, or population rules.
The direct sequence is forearms on wall, upward slide, top lift-off, forearms back to wall, then slide down.
Vortex adds explicit valid-repetition, fixed-foot, compensation, stop, persistence, and actual-duration rules without presenting them as source-validated treatment effects.

evidence.sourceTitle: Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy Diagnosis, Nonsurgical Medical Care, and Rehabilitation: A Clinical Practice Guideline
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Clinical diagnosis, medical care, rehabilitation, prognosis, and return-to-sport decisions require an appropriate professional context.
Stop and escalation rules must distinguish ordinary effort from sharp or escalating pain, neurologic symptoms, trauma, recurrent instability, cardiopulmonary symptoms, and other emergencies.

evidence.sourceTitle: The effects of wall slide and sling slide exercises on scapular alignment and pain in subjects with scapular downward rotation
claims: A small four-week study in 22 people with scapular downward rotation compared wall and sling slides and reported condition-specific changes.
The population, protocol, and no-lift-off task do not justify universal treatment, prevention, posture-correction, readiness, or performance claims for this card.
The direct page names wall setup, forearm contact, controlled upward motion, top lift-off, and controlled return.
Athlete support must explain expected light-to-moderate local effort, exact contacts and sequence, permitted range changes, unexpected symptoms, and how to stop and ask for help.

evidence.sourceTitle: Theraband Applications for Improved Upper Extremity Wall-Slide Exercises
claims: Wall-slide phase, shoulder angle, forearm orientation, contact, tempo, and resistance position materially define the tested task and muscle-activity context.
Coach support must observe the exact interface, path, first fault, actual exposure, downstream overhead demand, and escalation without diagnosing scapular pathology.
The source uses a wall and body position that can be explained with stepwise contact and direction prompts.

Smaller comfortable range, lower lift-off amplitude, slower tempo, fewer repetitions, visual checkpoint prompts, and a stable forearm comfort layer are annotations; omitting lift-off or changing base requires another card.

evidence.sourceTitle: Theraband Applications for Improved Upper Extremity Wall-Slide Exercises
claims: Band placement at the wrists or elbows changes muscle-activation patterns compared with a regular wall slide.
Resistance, interface, base, laterality, equipment, terminal action, or clinical purpose changes remain proposed variants or distinct definitions rather than silent annotations.

oEmbed health does not prove playback, exact forearm contacts, terminal full-arm lift-off, fixed feet, return count, captions, accessibility, cue quality, safety, reviewer identity, card-version match, or approval.
